source.title: How feature learning can improve neural scaling laws
source.authors: Blake Bordelon; Alexander Atanasov; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. It is not garbled or cut off in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains its own solvable and nonlinear networks and measures loss scaling under feature learning. Those results bear on versions about training behavior, although its central outcome is loss scaling rather than classification error.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own training and scaling results. Cited findings from other work are not rows. CIFAR-5M results are test-loss scaling curves, not training classification error.
record.test_reason: The study measures feature-learning effects on loss-scaling exponents. It does not test near-zero training classification error, spurious minima, depth degradation, signal-preserving initialization, learning-rate stability thresholds, or batch-normalization benefits. Its parameter γ controls feature learning, rather than measuring any listed version's mechanism.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that feature learning can improve time and compute scaling exponents for hard tasks outside the initial kernel's RKHS, while easy and super-easy tasks retain their exponents. They identify a late-time discrepancy on CIFAR-5M and emphasize that their theory assumes MSE and SGD; the transformer cross-entropy experiment is preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates scaling of test loss in a projected-gradient solvable model and deep nonlinear networks, not the classification-error outcomes in the listed claim versions. Its main vision experiments use enlarged MNIST-1M and CIFAR-5M datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Task difficulty β, feature-learning parameter γ or γ0, dataset, and training time affect the reported loss-scaling outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature learning improves time and compute scaling exponents for hard tasks outside the initial kernel's RKHS; easy tasks retain their asymptotic exponents. Synthetic nonlinear-network experiments follow these predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning can improve loss-scaling exponents when the target lies outside the initial kernel's RKHS.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST-1M test-loss scaling follows the predicted exponent; CIFAR-5M eventually improves faster than predicted, especially at larger γ0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning improves vision-task test-loss scaling, with departures from the solvable theory depending on dataset and training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: The transformer experiment reports roughly twice the loss-scaling exponent at large γ compared with small γ, with an approximate early-time theoretical fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning can improve early-time cross-entropy scaling in next-token prediction.

record.problems: The paper's evidence is primarily about test-loss scaling rather than training classification error. Its nonlinear vision experiments use MNIST-1M and CIFAR-5M, not the classification benchmarks and outcomes named in the versions. The authors report that CIFAR-5M eventually exhibits a better power law than their theory predicts. The supplied results do not state uncertainty for the specific Figure 5, Figure 6, or Figure 9 comparisons.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and model-size or regularization effects.
Spurious-minimum frequencies in two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks and their reduction with extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity-shortcut comparisons, and deep-network training with special initialization.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient preservation, orthogonal-versus-Gaussian training speed, and trainable depth.
Loss recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence thresholds.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T2 classification should be changed to discusses/T6. All five rows concern a related optimization outcome that fits none of V1–V6; their cannot_determine states do not indicate absent effects.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, or effects of model size on reaching near-zero training error.
No teacher-student ReLU local-minimum experiment or width comparison.
No comparison of plain and residual networks' training classification error or of shortcut effects.
No comparison of initialization schemes or trainable depth attributable to initialization.
No learning-rate stability-limit or sharpness experiment.
